newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrians silently view Nazi looted art.
newsitem.headline: Austrians silently view Nazi looted art.

text.p: An oil painting shows two children against a dreamy landscape, their arms around each other, entitled "Forever yours Mama and Papa".

"That probably once hung over the sofa in the sitting room," said a 70-year old woman, one of many visitors on Wednesday to an exhibition of Jewish art looted by Nazis in World War Two and currently on show in Vienna.

No-one has claimed the work and it is unlikely any member of the family that owned the painting survived the Holocaust. As with the other 8,000 artworks to come under the hammer on October 29 and 30, not even the owner's name is known.

The proceeds, estimated to reach around $3.5 million, will be given to Austrian victims of the Holocaust, including non-Jews. Communists, gypsies and homosexuals were also rounded up and ferried to Nazi death camps.
Peter Noever, director of the Vienna Museum for Applied Arts where the exhibition is being held, described the collection as "Stolen art from stolen lives".

"I can't bear to think how awful it must have been for those who had to give up all they had," said an art dealer, standing in front of a picture of a young woman lost in her thoughts surrounded by lilacs and roses.

Most of the 19th century paintings which graced Viennese sitting rooms before World War Two, depicted idyllic scenes with titles such as "Family happiness in the countryside" and "Deer grazing in the woods".
"It is hard to believe that the owners were all murdered," a woman in her 50s said.
A retired civil servant was impressed by the extensiveness of the collection, which was stored for over 40 years in a monastery in Mauerbach.
"It's interesting to see the kind of objects they collected then," he said. "There you see such a peaceful scene...but they could not know what would happen," he said.
A 78-year old woman and her friend, lured to the exhibition from a nearby Viennese coffee house, were reluctant to speak about Austria's Nazi past.
"It was a sad time then," one said. "It's a shame that so many people supported Hitler," said her companion.
All viewers spoken to declined to give their names.

After Hitler's German forces occupied Austria in 1938 Jewish households were systematically looted for artworks. The valuable pieces were marked as "reserved for the Fuehrer" and destined for a museum in Linz Hitler planned to erect.
"Here is displayed the legacy of those who were murdered, exiled and forgotten," said museum director Noever.
Most of the items are well-preserved. An entire Meissner porcelain coffee set with colourful dragons survived the war and four decades in storage in the monastery.
A 15th century painting by Sienese artist Pietro di Francesco degli Orioli, depicting the Madonna and child and valued up to $110,000, is expected to fetch the highest price.
"We represent those who can no longer be helped, because their lives were taken along with their possessions," said Paul Grosz, president of the Vienna Jewish community.
